newsitem.title: CHINA: China bank scholar calls for smaller forex reserve.
newsitem.headline: China bank scholar calls for smaller forex reserve.

text.p: A Chinese central bank researcher has called on Beijing to keep foreign exchange reserves of up to $60 billion, far less than the $100 billion reserves expected by the end of 1996, the Xinhua news agency said on Thursday.
China's foreign exchange reserves rose to $95.0 billion at the end of September, up about $20 billion since the beginning of the year, official figures show.

The expansion of China's foreign exchange reserves had in the past caused money supply problems and fuelled inflation, said Lin Zhiyuan of the Research Institute of Finance and Banking of the People's Bank of China, the central bank.

"Although a certain amount of foreign exchange reserves are necessary to ensure a country's viability, this does not mean that the more foreign exchange reserves there are, the better," the official Xinhua news agency quoted Lin as saying.

Under international financial practice, the ideal size of national reserves could be calculated from the combination of the amount of foreign currency needed to pay for imports for up to four months and 10 percent of foreign debt, Lin said.
"Based on this calculation, I believe that our country's foreign exchange reserves should stand somewhere between $50 billion and $60 billion," Xinhua quoted her as saying.
"The strong increase in foreign exchange reserves since 1994 has had a negative effect on the domestic money supply," she said.
China's expansion of its reserves had forced it to spend 566.2 billion yuan ($68 billion) on procuring foreign exchange in 1994 and 1995, helping to fuel high inflation, she said.
Xinhua said Lin expected China's foreign exchange reserves to grow by $30 billion during 1996, forcing the state to set aside another 250 billion yuan to buy foreign exchange.

There was no chance that China would use its massive foreign exchange reserves, expected to top $100 billion by the end of 1996, to manipulate the international foreign exchange market, she said, but gave no details.
